The gateway gives your containers real HTTPS addresses, such as https://shop.localhost , instead of http://localhost:8095 . This page covers how it works, where routes come from, certificates, custom domains and the landing page that lists everything you run.

The gateway is a Caddy container ( caddy:2 alpine , named orca gateway ) that Orca creates and configures for you. It listens on ports 80 and 443 of your machine, matches each request's hostname (and optionally its path) and forwards it to a port inside a container. Port 80 only redirects to HTTPS. Start it with Start gateway on the Gateway page, or orca gateway start . The first start pulls the image. After that the container comes back when Docker restarts, until you stop it with Stop gateway , which asks first because every gateway URL stops working until you start it again. Orca also start

The default domain is localhost . A route named shop becomes shop.localhost , and Chrome and Firefox send every .localhost name to your own machine without any DNS setup. Other programs (Safari, curl , scripts, test runners) use the system resolver, which may not resolve .localhost . The Worktrees page warns when an instance hostname doesn't resolve on your computer.

To use names that resolve everywhere, pick a domain with a wildcard DNS record pointing at 127.0.0.1 , such as .local.yourcompany.dev , and set it as the Domain on the Gateway page's Settings tab, under Domain and ports : Routes from orca.yaml and labels follow the new domain. Routes you added by hand keep the full hostname they were given. When you click Save settings (domain, ports, TLS) or change them with orca gateway config , a running gateway restarts with the new settings, so they apply at once.

The TLS mode under HTTPS on the Settings tab decides where certificates come from. Mode Orca CA (automatic) orca ca The default. Orca runs its own certificate authority and issues a certificate for every routed hostname and for the domain itself. Works with any domain and any hostname depth. Custom certificate custom You paste a certificate and private key in PEM format. Every route uses that one certificate, so it must cover all of your hostnames.

Browsers trust Orca's certificates once the Orca CA is in your system trust store. Install it from the command line: This runs sudo security add trusted cert into the System keychain on macOS, copies it to /usr/local/share/ca certificates/ and runs update ca certificates on Linux, and uses certutil on Windows. You can also download it from Settings → Certificates with Download CA certificate , which shows install instructions too. orca ca info prints its subject, expiry and fingerprint. The CA is created on first use and stored in Orca's config folder, under orca/ca/ .

A container that calls a gateway hostname over HTTPS needs to trust the CA as well. Write it out and mount it into the container: The certificate is also served without authentication at http://127.0.0.1:9477/api/v1/ca/certificate , which is handy in setup scripts. How a container uses it depends on the runtime; Node.js, for example, reads NODE EXTRA CA CERTS=/path/to/orca ca.pem .

With a custom wildcard certificate such as .local.yourcompany.dev , remember that a wildcard covers exactly one label. web feat x shop.local.yourcompany.dev is covered; web.feat x.shop.local.yourcompany.dev is not. Worktree instances use the flat form by default for this reason, and Orca warns when a planned instance hostname isn't covered by the gateway's certificate. See hostnames per instance.

Inside a container, a name like auth.localhost would normally point at the container itself. Orca fixes this: the gateway joins the networks of every routed container and carries every routed hostname as a network alias. Containers on those networks reach https://auth.localhost through the gateway, exactly as the browser does. This matters for OIDC issuer URLs and other server to server calls by public name. The calling container must trust the Orca CA for HTTPS to verify. The default bridge network has no DNS, so this works on compose and user defined networks only.

Worktree instances let every git worktree of a project run as its own copy of the app, side by side, each with its own URLs and ports. Databases, caches and other infrastructure run once in a shared stack that every worktree uses. In a compose template, every changeme in the compose YAML is replaced with one generated password for the whole stack, so the services that share a password (an app and its database) still match. Push to deploy lets a registry tell the Orca daemon that a new image exists. The daemon pulls it and recreates the matching containers with the new image. Use it on a server running orca daemon so that a git push ends with the new version running, with no SSH step in between.

1. Your CI pipeline builds an image and pushes it to a registry. 2. The registry sends a webhook to the daemon. 3. The daemon checks the signature, reads the image name and tag, and looks for deploy rules that match. 4. For each matching rule, it pulls image:tag in the background, then stops, removes and recreates each target container with the new image. This page explains how the Orca daemon authenticates requests, what it listens on, where secrets are stored, and which connections Orca makes to the outside world. Read it before exposing a daemon on a network or turning on the AI assistant.

Everything Orca does goes through the daemon's REST API. Every request needs the daemon's API token: The daemon generates the token on first start: 16 random bytes from the operating system's secure random number generator, written as 32 hex characters. Tokens are compared in constant time, so response timing doesn't reveal how much of a guess was right. WebSocket connections, used for terminals and the Kubernetes setup log, pass the token as a token query parameter instead of a header, and the daemon checks it the same way. A few routes don't take the API token: Route Why /api/v1/health Repor

The token is stored as api token in Orca's config.json : System Path Linux ~/.config/orca/config.json macOS ~/Library/Application Support/orca/config.json Windows %APPDATA%\orca\config.json Linux server package /etc/orca/config.json On Linux, /etc/orca/config.json takes precedence when it exists. On Linux and macOS the file is written with mode 600 , and the daemon logs a warning if it finds it readable by other users. To rotate the token, change or remove api token and restart the daemon. A missing token is regenerated on start.

The daemon listens on 127.0.0.1:9477 by default, so only programs on the same machine can reach it. The desktop app always starts it this way. The daemon speaks plain HTTP, which is fine on the loopback interface. You can change this with flags when you run orca daemon yourself: bind <ADDR listens on another address: an IPv4 or IPv6 address, or localhost . Any address that isn't a loopback address ( 127.0.0.1 , localhost , ::1 ) makes the daemon log WARNING: Daemon binding to <ADDR — the API will be network accessible! . socket <PATH listens on a Unix socket instead of TCP, created with mode 6

Each remote host has its own token, saved in plain text in the desktop app's config.json and sent only to that host. Verify TLS certificate is on by default for https:// hosts. Turn it off only for a self signed certificate you trust.

The gateway serves your containers over HTTPS with certificates signed by a local certificate authority that Orca creates the first time it needs one. The CA certificate and key are stored in orca/ca/ inside the config directory, for example ~/.config/orca/ca/ on Linux. The key is written with mode 600 and isn't encrypted. The CA is valid for 10 years. Certificates for gateway hostnames are stored in orca/ca/certs/ and are valid for one year. Orca never adds the CA to your system's trust store by itself. You do that from Settings , Certificates , with Download CA certificate and the command sh
